title: Слово о пълку Игоревѣ
titleEn: The Tale of Igor's Campaign — VI: The appeal to the princes
part: VI — The appeal to the princes
draftNote: Part VI — the second half of Svyatoslav's «золото слово» (Golden Word), begun at the end of part 5: his lament for his brother Yaroslav of Chernigov's scattered auxiliary troops, the mourning for Rimov/Urim and the wounded Vladimir Glebovich of Pereyaslavl, then a roll-call appeal in turn to the great princes of Rus' — Vsevolod 'Big Nest' of Suzdal, Rurik and David of Smolensk, Yaroslav Osmomysl of Galich, Roman and Mstislav of Volhynia, and Ingvar, Vsevolod and the three Mstislavichi — each summoned to avenge Igor. The movement is built on the refrain «за раны Игоревы... буего Святъславлича», sounded three times, and ends at its third and final sounding.
source: Text: editio princeps — «Ироическая пѣснь о походѣ на половцовъ удѣльнаго князя Новагорода-Сѣверскаго Игоря Святославича», ed. A. I. Musin-Pushkin, Moscow, 1800 (public domain); via Russian Wikisource. 1800 orthography preserved. Prose sense-units at the edition's punctuation (no imposed verse lineation). Transliteration: scholarly Slavist romanization (ž š č c x; ě = ѣ; ŭ / ĭ = ъ / ь). Pronunciation: reconstructed late-12th-c. Old East Slavic (see slovo-audio doc); ж/ш/ц read hard by convention. Translations made fresh from the 1800 original.
about: The second half of Svyatoslav's Golden Word, opened at the end of part 5. He first mourns what Igor's defeat has cost the Rus' more broadly — his brother Yaroslav of Chernigov's light auxiliary troops idle, the town of Urim (probably Rimov) sacked, Vladimir Glebovich of Pereyaslavl wounded defending his city — before turning to appeal, prince by prince, to the great powers of the Rus' lands to march and avenge Igor: Vsevolod 'Big Nest' of Suzdal-Vladimir, whose army could (the poet says) splash the Volga apart with oars; Rurik and David Rostislavich of Smolensk and Kiev; Yaroslav Osmomysl of Galich, guardian of the Hungarian frontier; Roman Mstislavich and his kinsman Mstislav of Volhynia, veterans of campaigns against Lithuania and the Yatvingians; and Ingvar, Vsevolod and the three Mstislavichi of the same Volhynian line. The appeal is carried by the poem's central refrain, «за раны Игоревы... буего Святъславлича» ('for the wounds of Igor, Svyatoslav's bold son'), sounded three times across the movement — twice as «Святславлича», once, at the close, as «Святъславлича» — a small, real spelling inconsistency of the 1800 print kept exactly as printed rather than normalized away. As throughout the poem, several words here are genuine hapax legomena found nowhere else in Old East Slavic (шереширы, папорзи, the place-name Деремела) and are flagged as unresolved rather than translated with invented confidence — the poem survives in no manuscript (the single copy burned in 1812), so no reading here claims more certainty than the 1800 print itself supports.

sentences.t: А уже не вижду власти сильнаго, и богатаго и многовои брата моего Ярослава съ Черниговьскими былями, съ Могуты и съ Татраны и съ Шельбиры, и съ Топчакы, исъ Ревугы, и съ Ольберы.
sentences.tr: A uže ne viždu vlasti silĭnago, i bogatago i mnogovoi brata moego Jaroslava sŭ Černigovĭskimi byljami, sŭ Moguty i sŭ Tatrany i sŭ Šelĭbiry, i sŭ Topčaky, isŭ Revugy, i sŭ Olĭbery.
sentences.l: And now I no longer see the might of my strong and rich and many-warriored brother Yaroslav, with the Chernigov elders, with the Mogutes and with the Tatrans and with the Shelbirs, and with the Topchaks, and with the Revugs, and with the Olbers.
sentences.i: And now I no longer see the power of my brother Yaroslav — strong, rich, and thronged with warriors — with his Chernigov elders, his Mogutes and Tatrans and Shelbirs, his Topchaks, his Revugs, his Olbers.
sentences.n: This continues Svyatoslav's Golden Word straight on from part 5's «Se li створисте...». «Брата моего Ярослава» is Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, prince of Chernigov (d. 1198), Svyatoslav's own younger brother — NOT the same man as the Yaroslav 'Osmomysl' of Galich addressed later in this part (unit 16); the poem names two different princes called Yaroslav within the same speech, an easy source of confusion for a modern reader. «былями» (instr. pl. of быль, an old word for a senior noble/elder, cf. боярин) names Chernigov's leading men; Могуты, Татраны, Шельбиры, Топчакы, Ревугы, Ольберы are names found nowhere else in Old East Slavic — generally taken to be Chernigov's auxiliary light-cavalry contingents of non-Slavic, probably Turkic, origin (tributary or allied nomadic groups serving the Chernigov princes), but their exact identity is genuinely unresolved.

sentences.t: Тіи бо бес щитовь съ засапожникы кликомъ плъкы побѣждаютъ, звонячи въ прадѣднюю славу.
sentences.tr: Tii bo bes ščitovĭ sŭ zasapožniky klikomŭ plŭky poběždajutŭ, zvonjači vŭ pradědnjuju slavu.
sentences.l: For these, without shields, with boot-knives, by their war-cry defeat armies, ringing out into ancestral glory.
sentences.i: These men, shieldless, armed only with knives tucked in their boots, rout whole armies with a war-cry, and ring out the fame of their forefathers.
sentences.n: засапожникы, 'boot-knives' (a knife carried за сапогомъ, 'behind/in the boot'), names a light, unconventional weapon: these auxiliaries fight without the standard shield, relying on surprise and the war-cry (кликомъ) alone. «звонячи въ прадѣднюю славу», 'ringing into ancestral glory,' pictures their fighting as itself sounding out the fame of earlier generations.

sentences.t: Нъ рекосте му жа имѣся сами, преднюю славу сами похитимъ, а заднюю ся сами подѣлимъ.
sentences.tr: Nŭ rekoste mu ža iměsja sami, prednjuju slavu sami poxitimŭ, a zadnjuju sja sami podělimŭ.
sentences.l: But you said, let-us-be-manly ourselves — the earlier glory we ourselves will seize, and the later glory we ourselves will divide.
sentences.i: But you said, 'Let us act like men, on our own' — the earlier glory we will seize for ourselves, and the rest we will share out among ourselves.
sentences.n: A famous crux. The standard reading takes «му жа имѣся» as one word, мужаимѣся, 'let us take heart, let us act like men' (from мужатисѧ); the 1800 print instead breaks the same letters into three pieces, kept here exactly as printed rather than silently rejoined. Svyatoslav quotes his nephews' own boast back at them — their resolve to win glory on their own, without him — as the root of the disaster. Note also the enclitic ся placed before its verb («заднюю ся ... подѣлимъ»), normal Old East Slavic word order but unlike modern Russian's fixed post-verbal -ся.

sentences.t: А чи диво ся братіе стару помолодити?
sentences.tr: A či divo sja bratie staru pomoloditi?
sentences.l: And is it any wonder, brothers, for an old man to grow young again?
sentences.i: And is it so strange, brothers, for an old man to find his youth again?
sentences.n: чи is an interrogative particle ('is it...?'); диво, 'wonder, marvel.' Svyatoslav poses a proverb-like riddle that the next sentence answers with the image of a molting falcon — though, as the sentence after that shows, the answer brings him no real comfort.

sentences.t: Коли соколъ въ мытехъ бываетъ, высоко птицъ възбиваетъ; не дастъ гнѣзда своего въ обиду.
sentences.tr: Koli sokolŭ vŭ mytexŭ byvaetŭ, vysoko pticŭ vŭzbivaetŭ; ne dastŭ gnězda svoego vŭ obidu.
sentences.l: When a falcon is in its molt, it drives the birds up high; it will not give its own nest over to harm.
sentences.i: When a falcon is molting, it still drives the other birds up high — it lets no harm come to its own nest.
sentences.n: мытехъ (loc. pl. of мыты) is the falconry term for a bird's molt, a period when a falcon might seem weaker but, the proverb says, is still dangerous and still guards its nest. This answers unit 4's riddle about an old man growing young — but Svyatoslav immediately turns the comparison against itself in the next sentence.

sentences.t: Нъ се зло Княже ми не пособіе; на ниче ся годины обратиша.
sentences.tr: Nŭ se zlo Knjaže mi ne posobie; na niče sja godiny obratiša.
sentences.l: But this, O Prince, is an evil, no help to me; to nothing have the times turned.
sentences.i: But that is small comfort to me, O Prince — the times have turned to nothing but ruin.
sentences.n: Svyatoslav turns the falcon-proverb back on itself: whatever comfort it offers in general, it is «зло» ('an evil') and «не пособіе» ('no help') to him now. «на ниче ся годины обратиша» places the reflexive particle ся before its verb обратиша ('turned') — ordinary Old East Slavic word order (the enclitic seeking second position in the clause), unlike modern Russian's fixed post-verbal -ся.

sentences.t: Се Уримъ кричатъ подъ саблями Половецкыми, а Володимиръ подъ ранами.
sentences.tr: Se Urimŭ kričatŭ podŭ sabljami Poloveckymi, a Volodimirŭ podŭ ranami.
sentences.l: Behold, Urim cry out under Polovtsian sabers, and Volodimir [lies] under wounds.
sentences.i: See how the men of Urim — probably Rimov — cry out under Polovtsian sabers, and Vladimir lies covered in wounds.
sentences.n: «Уримъ» is a genuine dark place — the word occurs nowhere else. The most often proposed reading takes it as a garbled reference to Римовъ (Rimov), a town near Pereyaslavl that the Hypatian Chronicle records as sacked by the Polovtsians in the immediate aftermath of Igor's 1185 defeat; on that reading, the line mourns Rimov's fall in the same breath as Volodimir's wounding. The identification is plausible but far from certain, and we flag it rather than assert it. «Володимиръ» is Vladimir Glebovich, prince of Pereyaslavl (see next unit), independently recorded by the Hypatian Chronicle as wounded defending his city in a Polovtsian raid that followed Igor's capture.

sentences.t: Туга и тоска сыну Глѣбову.
sentences.tr: Tuga i toska synu Glěbovu.
sentences.l: Anguish and heartache for Gleb's son.
sentences.i: Grief and heartache for the son of Gleb.
sentences.n: 'Gleb's son' is Vladimir Glebovich, prince of Pereyaslavl (d. 1187), son of Gleb Yuryevich — the same wounded prince named in the unit above; his wounding while defending Pereyaslavl after Igor's capture is recorded in the Hypatian Chronicle.

sentences.t: Великый Княже Всеволоде! не мыслію ти прелетѣти издалеча, отня злата стола поблюсти?
sentences.tr: Velikyj Knjaže Vsevolode! ne mysliju ti preletěti izdaleča, otnja zlata stola pobljusti?
sentences.l: Great Prince Vsevolod! is it not for you, in thought, to fly here from afar, to watch over your father's golden throne?
sentences.i: Great Prince Vsevolod! Could you not, even in thought, fly here from so far away, to keep watch over your father's golden throne?
sentences.n: A THIRD prince named Vsevolod in the poem — not Igor's brother 'Buy Tur' Vsevolod of parts 1–2, and not the Vsevolod Yaroslavich addressed later in this same part (unit 28) — but Vsevolod III Yuryevich of Vladimir-Suzdal, later nicknamed 'Big Nest' (Большое Гнѣздо) for his many children, the most powerful prince of the northeast and a cousin of Igor and Svyatoslav. «не мыслію ти прелетѣти» — 'could you not fly here in thought' — asks him to reach across the great distance from Suzdal at least in spirit. The exclamation mark is followed by a lower-case continuation in the print, a sign (as elsewhere in the poem) that the vocative address and the question that follows belong to one and the same sentence.

sentences.t: Ты бо можеши Волгу веслы раскропити, а Донъ шеломы выльяти.
sentences.tr: Ty bo možeši Volgu vesly raskropiti, a Donŭ šelomy vylĭjati.
sentences.l: For you can splash the Volga apart with oars, and pour the Don out with helmets.
sentences.i: You could splash the Volga apart with your oars, and empty the Don with helmets.
sentences.n: A hyperbole on the scale of Vsevolod's army — vast enough that its oars could churn the Volga apart and its helmets bail the Don dry — echoing, and outdoing, Igor's own vow «испити шеломомь Дону» ('to drink the Don with a helmet') from part 1.

sentences.t: Аже бы ты былъ, то была бы Чага по ногатѣ, а Кощей по резанѣ.
sentences.tr: Aže by ty bylŭ, to byla by Čaga po nogatě, a Koščej po rezaně.
sentences.l: If you had been [there], then a Chaga would have gone for a nogata, and a Koshchei for a rezana.
sentences.i: Had you been there, a captive girl would have sold for a nogata, and a captive man for a rezana.
sentences.n: One of the poem's clearest images. Чага and Кощей are old terms for a captive woman and a captive man respectively (кощей, from a Turkic word for a camp-servant or slave, is the same root that centuries later gave the unrelated folktale villain Koshchei the Deathless); ногата и резана are small units of the old Rus' monetary system, fractions of a grivna, the ногата worth somewhat more than the резана. The image: after such a victory, captives would be so plentiful they would sell for next to nothing.

sentences.t: Ты бо можеши посуху живыми шереширы стрѣляти удалыми сыны Глѣбовы.
sentences.tr: Ty bo možeši posuxu živymi šereširy strěljati udalymi syny Glěbovy.
sentences.l: For you can, over dry land, shoot living shereshiry — the daring sons of Gleb.
sentences.i: On dry land itself you can loose living 'shereshiry' — the daring sons of Gleb.
sentences.n: шереширъ is a genuine hapax legomenon, found nowhere else in Old East Slavic; its meaning is unresolved. Proposals range from a kind of arrow or dart to an incendiary projectile, possibly a borrowing tied to a Turkic or Persian military term — we flag it as a true dark place rather than assert a meaning. Here living warriors — 'the sons of Gleb,' usually identified as the princes of Ryazan, sons of Gleb Rostislavich of Ryazan (d. 1178), whom the Suzdal princes brought under their authority in the 1180s — are figured as human projectiles Vsevolod can loose even without a river to cross, continuing the Volga/Don hyperbole of the previous unit.

sentences.t: Ты буй Рюриче и Давыде, не ваю ли злачеными шеломы по крови плаваша?
sentences.tr: Ty buj Rjuriče i Davyde, ne vaju li zlačenymi šelomy po krovi plavaša?
sentences.l: You, fierce Rurik and David, was it not your two gilded helmets that swam in blood?
sentences.i: You, bold Rurik and David — did your gilded helmets not once swim in blood?
sentences.n: Addresses Rurik Rostislavich, who held Kiev jointly with Svyatoslav in these years, and his brother David Rostislavich, prince of Smolensk — senior princes of the Smolensk branch of the Rurikids and seasoned campaigners against the Polovtsians. ваю is a true dual ('of you two'); плаваша carries the plural aorist ending (cf. рекосте, расхытисте elsewhere in this part) — it agrees grammatically with the plural шеломы, not a dual form, though it still refers to the pair's own helmets.

sentences.t: Не ваю ли храбрая дружина рыкаютъ акы тури, ранены саблями калеными, на полѣ незнаемѣ?
sentences.tr: Ne vaju li xrabraja družina rykajutŭ aky turi, raneny sabljami kalenymi, na polě neznaemě?
sentences.l: Was it not your brave druzhina that roars like wild bulls, wounded by tempered sabers, on the unknown field?
sentences.i: Was it not your brave men who roared like aurochs, wounded by hardened sabers, on some unknown field?
sentences.n: акы тури, 'like aurochs, wild bulls' — the same animal behind Vsevolod 'Buy Tur's epithet in part 1 — pictures the warriors' battle-roar. «на полѣ незнаемѣ», 'on an unknown field,' is a recurring epic formula for a distant, unnamed battlefield rather than one specific named engagement.

sentences.t: Вступита Господина въ злата стремень за обиду сего времени, за землю Русскую, за раны Игоревы, буего Святславлича!
sentences.tr: Vstupita Gospodina vŭ zlata stremenĭ za obidu sego vremeni, za zemlju Russkuju, za rany Igorevy, buego Svjatslavliča!
sentences.l: Step, [you two] lords, into the golden stirrup, for the insult of this time, for the Russian land, for the wounds of Igor, bold son of Svyatoslav!
sentences.i: Mount, my lords, into your golden stirrups — for the wrong done in these times, for the Russian land, for the wounds of Igor, Svyatoslav's bold son!
sentences.n: The first sounding, within part 6, of the poem's great refrain «за раны Игоревы... буего Святъславлича», addressed to Rurik and David (Вступита is a 2nd-person DUAL imperative, 'you two, step/mount'). «въ злата стремень» repeats the set formula used of Igor himself in part 1. Here, and again in unit 19, the refrain is printed «Святславлича» — without the о after т and without ъ — unlike its third and final sounding at the very end of this part, printed «Святъславлича» with ъ; a small, real spelling inconsistency of the 1800 print, kept exactly as printed each time rather than normalized.

sentences.t: Галичкы Осмомыслѣ Ярославе высоко сѣдиши на своемъ златокованнѣмъ столѣ.
sentences.tr: Galičky Osmomyslě Jaroslave vysoko sědiši na svoemŭ zlatokovanněmŭ stolě.
sentences.l: O Yaroslav of Galich, Eight-Minded one, high do you sit upon your gold-forged throne.
sentences.i: O Yaroslav of Galich, wise Osmomysl! High you sit upon your golden throne.
sentences.n: A different Yaroslav from unit 1's brother of Svyatoslav — this is Yaroslav Vladimirkovich of Galich (r. 1153–1187), one of the wealthiest and most powerful princes of the age. His epithet Осмомыслъ ('eight-minded,' i.e. of many wits) is first recorded here; its precise sense is debated but it is generally read as praise for extraordinary sagacity. Galich lay in the far southwest, on the upper Dniester near the Carpathians, which is why the following unit pictures him guarding the Hungarian frontier.

sentences.t: Подперъ горы Угорскыи своими желѣзными плъки, заступивъ Королеви путь, затвори въ Дунаю ворота, меча времены чрезъ облаки, суды рядя до Дуная.
sentences.tr: Podperŭ gory Ugorskyi svoimi želěznymi plŭky, zastupivŭ Korolevi putĭ, zatvori vŭ Dunaju vorota, meča vremeny črezŭ oblaki, sudy rjadja do Dunaja.
sentences.l: Having propped up the Hungarian mountains with your iron regiments, having barred the King's way, having shut the gates at the Danube, hurling times through the clouds, ordering judgments as far as the Danube.
sentences.i: You prop up the Hungarian mountains with your iron regiments, bar the King's road, shut the gates on the Danube, hurl your power through the very clouds, and hand down judgment as far as the Danube.
sentences.n: «Королеви», 'the King's,' uses король, a word ultimately from the name Charlemagne and applied in Old Rus' texts to Western, Catholic monarchs — almost certainly the King of Hungary here, whose realm bordered Galich across the Carpathians. «меча времены чрезъ облаки» is itself a well-known crux: времены ('times') sits oddly as the object of 'hurling... through the clouds,' and it is often read as a print corruption of бремены ('loads, weights,' i.e. projectiles — fitting an image of siege engines throwing stones sky-high); we keep the 1800 print's wording in t and l, and flag the difficulty rather than silently emend it.

sentences.t: Грозы твоя по землямъ текутъ; оттворяеши Кіеву врата; стрѣляеши съ отня злата стола Салтани за землями.
sentences.tr: Grozy tvoja po zemljamŭ tekutŭ; ottvorjaeši Kievu vrata; strěljaeši sŭ otnja zlata stola Saltani za zemljami.
sentences.l: Your terrors flow across the lands; you open Kiev's gates; you shoot Sultans beyond the lands from your father's golden throne.
sentences.i: Your fearsome name runs through every land; you throw open the gates of Kiev; from your father's golden throne you strike at Sultans far beyond your borders.
sentences.n: «оттворяеши Кіеву врата», 'you open Kiev's gates,' credits Yaroslav with real influence over who held Kiev, reflecting Galich's genuine weight in Kievan politics of the period. «стрѣляеши... Салтани за землями», 'you shoot Sultans beyond the lands,' is usually taken as panegyric hyperbole about the reach of his power rather than a literal war against a named Muslim ruler — though it may echo Galich's real, independently attested links westward and toward Byzantium: Yaroslav sheltered the future Byzantine emperor Andronikos I Komnenos at his court in the 1160s, an episode recorded by the Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates.

sentences.t: Стрѣляй Господине Кончака, поганого Кощея за землю Рускую, за раны Игоревы буего Святславлича.
sentences.tr: Strěljaj Gospodine Končaka, poganogo Koščeja za zemlju Ruskuju, za rany Igorevy buego Svjatslavliča.
sentences.l: Shoot, O lord, [at] Konchak, the pagan Koshchei, for the Russian land, for the wounds of Igor, bold son of Svyatoslav.
sentences.i: Take aim, my lord, at Konchak, that pagan slave-taker, for the sake of the Russian land, for the wounds of Igor, Svyatoslav's bold son.
sentences.n: The second sounding of the refrain, now naming Konchak directly — the historical Polovtsian khan who, together with Gzak, defeated and captured Igor in 1185 and went on to raid the Pereyaslavl region (see units 7–8). Кощей is reused from unit 11, there for an ordinary captive, here as an insult for Konchak himself: 'the [pagan] slave-taker/captor.'

sentences.t: А ты буй Романе и Мстиславе! храбрая мысль носитъ васъ умъ на дѣло.
sentences.tr: A ty buj Romane i Mstislave! xrabraja myslĭ nositŭ vasŭ umŭ na dělo.
sentences.l: And you, fierce Roman and Mstislav! brave thought carries your mind to action.
sentences.i: And you, bold Roman and Mstislav — brave thoughts drive your minds to action.
sentences.n: Roman is Roman Mstislavich, prince of Volhynia from 1170 and, from 1199, founder of the united Galicia-Volhynia principality — one of the major Rus' princes of the next generation. The Mstislav named beside him is not securely identified; he is usually taken to be a kinsman of Roman's from the same Volhynian branch (compare unit 28), but the text itself does not say which one, and we do not claim more certainty than that.

sentences.t: Высоко плаваеши на дѣло въ буести, яко соколъ на вѣтрехъ ширяяся, хотя птицю въ буйствѣ одолѣти.
sentences.tr: Vysoko plavaeši na dělo vŭ buesti, jako sokolŭ na větrexŭ širjajasja, xotja pticju vŭ bujstvě odolěti.
sentences.l: High do you soar to action in your fierce daring, like a falcon rising on the winds, wishing in his fury to overcome a bird.
sentences.i: You soar to battle high on your own daring, like a falcon riding the winds, bent on bringing down its prey.
sentences.n: Continues the falcon-image already used of Boyan (proem) and of Igor's own warriors (part 1, «Не буря соколы занесе...»), here applied to Roman and Mstislav's eagerness for battle; part 1's Kurians, by contrast, are pictured as grey wolves, not falcons.

sentences.t: Суть бо у ваю желѣзныи папорзи подъ шеломы латинскими.
sentences.tr: Sutĭ bo u vaju želěznyi paporzi podŭ šelomy latinskimi.
sentences.l: For you two have iron paporzi under Latin helmets.
sentences.i: The two of you wear iron paporzi beneath your Western-style helmets.
sentences.n: папорзи is another rare, disputed word; proposals include a mail neck-guard (aventail) fixed to the helmet and, alternatively, straps or fastenings (related to поворозы) that secured it — the exact form and sense remain unresolved. «шеломы латинскими», 'Latin [Western European, Catholic] helmets,' fits Volhynia's position on the Polish and Hungarian frontier, where Western-style armor and alliances lay closer at hand than in the Rus' heartland.

sentences.t: Тѣми тресну земля, и многи страны Хинова.
sentences.tr: Těmi tresnu zemlja, i mnogi strany Xinova.
sentences.l: By these the earth resounded, and many lands — [even] Khinova.
sentences.i: At this the earth itself shook, and it was heard in many lands, even distant Khinova.
sentences.n: Хинова, also met in part 5 («великое буйство подасть Хинови»), names a distant, half-legendary people or land at the edge of the known world; whether it preserves a folk-memory of the Huns or reflects a later use of the name for a far-eastern land is not settled, and we flag the uncertainty rather than resolve it.

sentences.t: Литва, Ятвязи, Деремела, и Половци сулици своя повръгоща, а главы своя поклониша подъ тыи мечи харалужныи.
sentences.tr: Litva, Jatvjazi, Deremela, i Polovci sulici svoja povrŭgošča, a glavy svoja pokloniša podŭ tyi meči xaralužnyi.
sentences.l: Lithuania, the Yatvingians, Deremela, and the Polovtsians cast down their javelins, and bowed their own heads under those kharalug swords.
sentences.i: Lithuania, the Yatvingians, the Deremela, and the Polovtsians all threw down their spears and bowed their heads beneath those hardened kharalug blades.
sentences.n: Литва and Ятвязи are real, well-attested Baltic peoples — the Lithuanians and the Yatvingians (a Baltic tribal group, close kin of the Old Prussians, settled between Poland and Lithuania) — both of whom Roman Mstislavich is independently recorded, in later chronicle entries, as having campaigned against as prince of Volhynia. Деремела, by contrast, is otherwise unattested; it is usually guessed to be another, smaller Baltic tribal group, but the name cannot be securely identified. харалужныи, 'of kharalug [steel],' is the poem's recurring word for an especially hard, legendary steel (parts 2–5).

sentences.t: Нъ уже Княже Игорю, утрпѣ солнцю свѣтъ, а древо не бологомъ листвіе срони: по Рсіи, по Сули гради подѣлиша; а Игорева храбраго плъку не крѣсити.
sentences.tr: Nŭ uže Knjaže Igorju, utrpě solncju světŭ, a drevo ne bologomŭ listvie sroni: po Rsii, po Suli gradi poděliša; a Igoreva xrabrago plŭku ne krěsiti.
sentences.l: But now, Prince Igor, the sun's light has grown dim, and the tree, not for good, has shed its leaves: along the Ros, along the Sula they have divided up the towns; and Igor's brave host cannot be raised.
sentences.i: But now, Prince Igor, the sun's light has faded, and the tree has shed its leaves — and not for any good: along the Ros and the Sula the towns have been carved up, and Igor's brave army cannot be brought back to life.
sentences.n: After the long roll-call of mighty allies, the poet turns back to the bare present. The sun-darkening image recalls the eclipse of part 1, and «не бологомъ» ('not for good, inauspiciously') marks the falling leaves as an ill omen rather than a season. Рсіи (the river Ros) and Сули (the Sula) are both real rivers just south of Kiev, the frontier zone most exposed to Polovtsian raiding. «не крѣсити» ('cannot be raised, resurrected' — крѣсити, cognate with воскресение, 'resurrection') states Igor's defeat as final, in stark contrast to everything just promised of the other princes.

sentences.t: Донъ ти Княже кличетъ, и зоветь Князи на побѣду.
sentences.tr: Donŭ ti Knjaže kličetŭ, i zovetĭ Knjazi na pobědu.
sentences.l: The Don, O Prince, calls to you, and summons the princes to victory.
sentences.i: The Don itself calls out to you, O Prince, summoning the princes on to victory.
sentences.n: The river is personified as calling the Rus' princes to march and avenge Igor, echoing the Don-refrain running through the poem since Igor's own vow in part 1.

sentences.t: Олговичи храбрыи Князи доспѣли на брань.
sentences.tr: Olgoviči xrabryi Knjazi dospěli na branĭ.
sentences.l: The brave Olgovichi princes have made ready for battle.
sentences.i: The bold Olgovichi princes stand ready for battle.
sentences.n: Олговичи, 'the sons/descendants of Oleg,' names the whole Chernigov branch of the Rurikids — descendants of Oleg Svyatoslavich, 'Gorislavich' (part 3) — to which Igor, Vsevolod, Svyatoslav III, and unit 1's Yaroslav of Chernigov all belong; the poet reports them collectively as prepared to fight.

sentences.t: Инъгварь и Всеволодъ, и вси три Мстиславичи, не худа гнѣзда шестокрилци, непобѣдными жребіи собѣ власти расхытисте?
sentences.tr: Inŭgvarĭ i Vsevolodŭ, i vsi tri Mstislaviči, ne xuda gnězda šestokrilci, nepobědnymi žrebii sobě vlasti rasxytiste?
sentences.l: Ingvar and Vsevolod, and all three Mstislavichi — [you] not of a poor nest, six-winged ones — did you not, by unconquered lots, seize power for yourselves?
sentences.i: Ingvar and Vsevolod, and all three sons of Mstislav — no mean brood you, you six-winged ones — did you not win your lands by a fortune no one could defeat?
sentences.n: A FOURTH prince named Vsevolod in the poem (compare units 9 and, in part 1, 'Buy Tur' Vsevolod): this one is Vsevolod Yaroslavich, together with his brother Ingvar Yaroslavich — princes of the Lutsk/Dorogobuzh line in Volhynia, grandsons of Iziaslav Mstislavich of Kiev. 'The three Mstislavichi' are their cousins, usually taken as sons of Iziaslav's other son, Mstislav Iziaslavich — the same Volhynian branch as Roman (unit 20), and NOT the separate Polotsk dynasty descended from Vseslav, met later in part 7; the exact identity of the three brothers is debated, and we do not claim more precision than that. «не худа гнѣзда», 'not of a poor nest,' is a litotes praising their lineage; шестокрилци, 'six-winged ones,' most likely echoes the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6 (familiar from Orthodox liturgy and icon-painting) as an exalted epithet for the group, rather than a literal count of six princes. расхытисте again carries the plural aorist ending, here for a group of five, not a true dual.

sentences.t: Кое ваши златыи шеломы и сулицы Ляцкіи и щиты!
sentences.tr: Koe vaši zlatyi šelomy i sulicy Ljackii i ščity!
sentences.l: Where are your golden helmets, and your Lyakh javelins, and shields!
sentences.i: Where now are your golden helmets, your Polish lances, your shields!
sentences.n: Ляцкіи, 'Lyakh, Polish' (from Ляхъ, the old term for a Pole), points to the same western military contacts noted for Volhynia in unit 22 — Polish-style weapons, or Polish allies, within reach of these princes.

sentences.t: Загородите полю ворота своими острыми стрѣлами за землю Русскую, за раны Игоревы буего Святъславлича.
sentences.tr: Zagorodite polju vorota svoimi ostrymi strělami za zemlju Russkuju, za rany Igorevy buego Svjatŭslavliča.
sentences.l: Bar the gate of the field with your sharp arrows, for the Russian land, for the wounds of Igor, bold son of Svyatoslav.
sentences.i: Wall off the open field with your sharp arrows — for the Russian land, for the wounds of Igor, Svyatoslav's bold son.
sentences.n: The refrain's third and final sounding, closing part 6 — printed this time with ъ, «Святъславлича», unlike its two earlier occurrences in this part (units 15 and 19), both printed without it, «Святславлича»; one more small, real orthographic inconsistency of the 1800 print, kept exactly as it stands rather than normalized away. «Загородите полю ворота», 'bar the gate to the field' (i.e. seal off the open steppe), closes the whole appeal with one concrete image: wall the frontier with arrows and avenge Igor.

glossary.вижду: видѣти — I see (1st sg. pres.); with не, 'I no longer see'
glossary.власти: власть — might, power(s) (gen. sg. in unit 1, object of negated вижду; acc. pl. in unit 28, 'seize power(s) for yourselves')
glossary.сильнаго: сильный — strong, mighty (gen. sg., agreeing with брата)
glossary.богатаго: богатый — rich (gen. sg., agreeing with брата)
glossary.многовои: многовои — many-warriored, thronged with warriors (gen. sg., agreeing with брата); a compound adjective (много 'many' + вои 'warriors')
glossary.моего: мой — my (gen. sg., agreeing with брата)
glossary.ярослава: Ярославъ — Yaroslav (gen. sg.); Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, prince of Chernigov (d. 1198), Svyatoslav's own brother — distinct from Yaroslav 'Osmomysl' of Galich addressed later in this part (unit 16), see note
glossary.былями: быль — elders, senior nobles (instr. pl.); an old word for a senior noble, cf. боярин
glossary.могуты: Могуты — the Mogutes (instr. pl.); an auxiliary light-cavalry group of Chernigov, of non-Slavic, probably Turkic origin, otherwise unattested (see note)
glossary.татраны: Татраны — the Tatrans (instr. pl.); ditto, otherwise unattested (see note)
glossary.шельбиры: Шельбиры — the Shelbirs (instr. pl.); ditto, otherwise unattested (see note)
glossary.топчакы: Топчакы — the Topchaks (instr. pl.); ditto, otherwise unattested (see note)
glossary.исъ: исъ — and with (prep.; = и + съ, a fused/variant spelling)
glossary.ревугы: Ревугы — the Revugs (instr. pl.); ditto, otherwise unattested (see note)
glossary.ольберы: Ольберы — the Olbers (instr. pl.); ditto, otherwise unattested (see note)
glossary.тіи: тъ — these, those (dem. pron., nom. pl.)
glossary.бес: безъ — without (prep. + gen.; spelled бес by assimilation before щ)
glossary.засапожникы: засапожникъ — boot-knife (instr. pl.); a knife carried за сапогомъ, 'behind/in the boot' (see note)
glossary.кликомъ: кликъ — with a cry, a shout (instr. sg.)
glossary.прадѣднюю: прадѣднии — ancestral (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with славу)
glossary.рекосте: рещи — you [pl.] said (aorist 2pl); Svyatoslav quotes his nephews' own boast back at them
glossary.му: мужаимѣся (as printed: му жа имѣся) — let us take heart, act like men! (1st pl. hortative, reflexive); the standard reading joins these three print-tokens into one word, мужаимѣся, kept split here as the 1800 print has it (see note)
glossary.жа: мужаимѣся (as printed: му жа имѣся) — let us take heart, act like men! (1st pl. hortative, reflexive); second of the three print-tokens usually rejoined into мужаимѣся (see note)
glossary.имѣся: мужаимѣся (as printed: му жа имѣся) — let us take heart, act like men! (1st pl. hortative, reflexive); third of the three print-tokens, carrying the reflexive ся, usually rejoined into мужаимѣся (see note)
glossary.сами: самъ — ourselves (nom. pl.); Svyatoslav quotes his nephews' own words
glossary.преднюю: предьнии — earlier, foremost (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with славу)
glossary.похитимъ: похитити — we will seize (1st pl. fut./pres.)
glossary.заднюю: задьнии — later, latter, remaining (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with an implied славу)
glossary.ся: ся — -self, reflexive particle (enclitic); placed before its verb, normal Old East Slavic word order (see note)
glossary.подѣлимъ: подѣлити — we will divide (1st pl. fut./pres.)
glossary.стару: старъ — an old man (dat. sg., short-form adj. used substantively)
glossary.помолодити: помолодити — to grow young again, regain one's youth (infinitive)
glossary.мытехъ: мыты — molt (loc. pl.); the falconry term for a bird's molt (see note)
glossary.възбиваетъ: възбивати — drives up, sends flying up (3rd sg. pres.)
glossary.ми: азъ — to me, for me (dat. sg. enclitic)
glossary.се: се — this (dem. pron.); also 'behold, lo' as a particle
glossary.уримъ: Уримъ — Urim (nom.); a genuine dark place, the word occurs nowhere else — most often taken as a garbled reference to Римовъ (Rimov), a town near Pereyaslavl recorded as sacked by the Polovtsians after Igor's defeat, but far from certain (see note); takes the plural verb кричатъ as a collective
glossary.володимиръ: Володимиръ — Vladimir (nom. sg.); Vladimir Glebovich, prince of Pereyaslavl, independently recorded by the Hypatian Chronicle as wounded defending his city after Igor's capture (see note)
glossary.глѣбову: Глѣбовъ — Gleb's (possessive adj., dat. sg.); Vladimir Glebovich, prince of Pereyaslavl (d. 1187), son of Gleb Yuryevich (see note)
glossary.всеволоде: Всеволодъ — Vsevolod! (vocative); Vsevolod III Yuryevich of Vladimir-Suzdal, later 'Big Nest' — a THIRD prince of this name in the poem, distinct from Igor's brother Vsevolod and from the Vsevolod Yaroslavich of unit 28 (see note)
glossary.ти: ты — for you, to you (dat. sg., enclitic)
glossary.прелетѣти: прелетѣти — to fly over, to fly here (infinitive)
glossary.поблюсти: поблюсти — to watch over, to guard (infinitive)
glossary.можеши: мочи — you can, you are able (2nd sg. pres.)
glossary.волгу: Влъга — the Volga (acc. sg.); the river
glossary.раскропити: раскропити — to splash apart, to spatter (infinitive)
glossary.донъ: Донъ — the Don (acc. sg. in unit 10, 'the Don... with helmets'; nom. sg. in unit 26, 'the Don calls'); the river
glossary.шеломы: шеломъ — helmets (instr. pl. in units 10, 22, 'with/under helmets'; nom. pl. in units 13, 29, functioning as grammatical subject — see note on the plural, not dual, ending of плаваша)
glossary.былъ: быти — had been, were (l-participle, masc. sg.)
glossary.чага: чага — a captive woman (nom. sg.); an old term for a female captive (see note)
glossary.по: по — along, over, according to; at, for [a price] (prep. + loc./dat.; sense varies by context)
glossary.ногатѣ: ногата — a nogata (loc. sg.); a small unit of the old Rus' monetary system, a fraction of a grivna (see note)
glossary.кощей: кощей — a captive man (nom. sg.); an old term for a male captive, from a Turkic word for a camp-servant/slave (see note)
glossary.резанѣ: рѣзана — a rezana (loc. sg.); a small monetary unit, smaller than a nogata (see note)
glossary.шереширы: шереширъ — shereshiry (instr. pl.); a genuine hapax legomenon, found nowhere else — proposals range from a kind of arrow or dart to an incendiary projectile, possibly a Turkic or Persian loanword; unresolved (see note)
glossary.глѣбовы: Глѣбовъ — Gleb's (possessive adj., acc. pl.); usually identified as the princes of Ryazan, sons of Gleb Rostislavich of Ryazan (d. 1178) (see note)
glossary.рюриче: Рюрикъ — Rurik! (vocative); Rurik Rostislavich, who held Kiev jointly with Svyatoslav in these years (see note)
glossary.давыде: Давыдъ — David! (vocative); David Rostislavich, prince of Smolensk, Rurik's brother (see note)
glossary.ваю: вы — of/for you two, your (gen./dat. dual)
glossary.плаваша: плавати — swam (aorist 3pl; agrees grammatically with the plural шеломы, not a dual form — see note)
glossary.храбрая: храбрый — brave (nom. sg. fem.; agrees with дружина in unit 14, with мысль in unit 20)
glossary.дружина: дружина — druzhina, war-band, retinue (nom. sg., a collective noun taking the plural verb рыкаютъ)
glossary.тури: туръ — aurochs, wild bulls (nom. pl., in the simile 'roar like aurochs'; cf. Vsevolod's epithet Буй Туръ, part 1)
glossary.ранены: раненъ — wounded (nom. pl., short-form past passive participle)
glossary.незнаемѣ: незнаемый — unknown (loc. sg., agreeing with полѣ); a recurring epic formula for a distant, unnamed battlefield
glossary.вступита: въступити — step! mount! (2nd dual imperative, addressed to Rurik and David)
glossary.за: за — for, for the sake of; behind, beyond (prep.)
glossary.русскую: руськый — Russian, of Rus' (acc. sg. fem., adj.); spelled with double с here, unlike рускую (single с) elsewhere in this part — a spelling variant kept as printed
glossary.буего: буй — bold, fierce (gen. sg., agreeing with Святославлича)
glossary.святславлича: Святъславличь — Svyatoslavich, son of Svyatoslav (gen. sg.); patronymic; spelled here without о after т and without ъ, «Святславлича» — the refrain's first and second soundings (units 15, 19), unlike its third and final sounding «Святъславлича» with ъ (unit 30) — a small, real spelling inconsistency of the 1800 print, kept exactly as printed (see note)
glossary.галичкы: Галичкый — of Galich (voc. sg. masc., adj.)
glossary.осмомыслѣ: Осмомыслъ — Eight-Minded, Osmomysl (voc. sg.); epithet of Yaroslav of Galich, first recorded here, generally read as praise for extraordinary sagacity (see note)
glossary.ярославе: Ярославъ — Yaroslav! (vocative); Yaroslav Vladimirkovich 'Osmomysl' of Galich (r. 1153–1187) — a different Yaroslav from unit 1's brother of Svyatoslav (see note)
glossary.подперъ: подперети — propped up (aorist 3sg / past active participle)
glossary.заступивъ: заступити — having barred (aorist / past active participle)
glossary.королеви: король — the King's (gen. sg.; король, ultimately from the name Charlemagne, applied to Western, Catholic monarchs — almost certainly the King of Hungary here, see note)
glossary.дунаю: Дунай — the Danube (loc. sg. in unit 17, 'at the Danube'; gen. sg. later in the same unit, 'as far as the Danube'); the river
glossary.меча: метати — hurling, throwing (present participle, nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.времены: время — times (acc. pl.); often read as a print corruption of бремены, 'loads, weights' (i.e. projectiles) — a genuine crux, kept as printed (see note)
glossary.рядя: рядити — ordering, arranging (present participle, nom. sg. masc.)
glossary.до: до — up to, as far as (prep. + gen.)
glossary.дуная: Дунай — the Danube (gen. sg.); the river
glossary.салтани: салтанъ — Sultans (acc. pl.); rulers of a Muslim state, taken as panegyric hyperbole about the reach of Yaroslav's power rather than a literal war (see note)
glossary.кончака: Кончакъ — Konchak (acc. sg.); the historical Polovtsian khan who, with Gzak, defeated and captured Igor in 1185 and went on to raid the Pereyaslavl region (see note)
glossary.кощея: кощей — slave-taker, captor (acc. sg.); reused here as an insult for Konchak himself, unlike its ordinary sense 'captive man' in unit 11 (see note)
glossary.рускую: руськый — Russian, of Rus' (acc. sg. fem., adj.)
glossary.романе: Романъ — Roman! (vocative); Roman Mstislavich, prince of Volhynia from 1170 and, from 1199, founder of Galicia-Volhynia (see note)
glossary.мстиславе: Мстиславъ — Mstislav! (vocative); a kinsman of Roman's from the same Volhynian branch, not securely identified (see note)
glossary.васъ: вы — your (gen. pl., possessive use, 'your mind')
glossary.плаваеши: плавати — you soar (2nd sg. pres.); lit. 'swim/float', of a falcon riding the wind
glossary.у: у — at, by, near (prep. + gen.); with ваю, 'you two have'
glossary.папорзи: папорзи — paporzi (nom. pl.); a disputed hapax — proposals include a mail neck-guard (aventail) fixed to the helmet, or alternatively straps/fastenings (related to поворозы) that secured it; unresolved (see note)
glossary.латинскими: латиньскый — Latin, Western European (instr. pl., adj.)
glossary.тѣми: тъ — by these (instr. pl., dem. pron.)
glossary.хинова: Хинова — Khinova (nom. sg.); an obscure, half-legendary distant people or land at the edge of the known world, also met in part 5 (dat. Хинови) — whether it preserves a folk-memory of the Huns or a later name for a far-eastern land is unresolved (see note)
glossary.литва: Литва — Lithuania (nom. sg.); a well-attested Baltic people, whom Roman Mstislavich is independently recorded as having campaigned against (see note)
glossary.ятвязи: Ятвязи — the Yatvingians (nom. pl.); a Baltic tribal group, close kin of the Old Prussians, settled between Poland and Lithuania (see note)
glossary.деремела: Деремела — Deremela (nom.); otherwise unattested, usually guessed to be another, smaller Baltic tribal group, but the name cannot be securely identified (see note)
glossary.своя: свой — his own; their own (acc. pl.)
glossary.харалужныи: харалужный — of kharalug [steel] (acc. pl., agreeing with мечи); the poem's recurring word for an especially hard, legendary steel (parts 2–5)
glossary.солнцю: сълньце — the sun's (dat. sg., possessive dative, 'the sun's light')
glossary.бологомъ: боlogo — good, weal (instr. sg.; 'не бологомъ' = 'not for good, inauspiciously')
glossary.рсіи: Рсь / Рсія — the Ros (loc. sg.); a river just south of Kiev, in the frontier zone exposed to Polovtsian raiding (see note)
glossary.сули: Сула — the Sula (loc. sg.); a river just south of Kiev, in the same frontier zone (see note)
glossary.храбраго: храбрый — brave (gen. sg., agreeing with плъку)
glossary.плъку: пълкъ — army, host (gen. sg., genitive of negation with не крѣсити)
glossary.крѣсити: крѣсити — to revive, to raise up (infinitive); cf. modern воскресение 'resurrection'
glossary.кличетъ: кликати — cries, calls (3sg); the Don personified, calling the Rus' princes to march (see note)
glossary.князи: кънязь — princes (acc. pl. in unit 26, object of зоветь; nom. pl. in unit 27, in apposition to Олговичи)
glossary.олговичи: Олговичи — the Olgovichi (nom. pl.); 'the sons/descendants of Oleg,' the whole Chernigov branch of the Rurikids, descendants of Oleg Svyatoslavich 'Gorislavich' (part 3) (see note)
glossary.доспѣли: доспѣти — have made ready, are prepared (past tense/l-participle, pl.)
glossary.инъгварь: Ингварь — Ingvar (nom. sg.); Ingvar Yaroslavich, prince of the Lutsk/Dorogobuzh line in Volhynia, grandson of Iziaslav Mstislavich of Kiev (see note)
glossary.всеволодъ: Всеволодъ — Vsevolod (nom. sg.); Vsevolod Yaroslavich, Ingvar's brother — a FOURTH prince of this name in the poem, distinct from Igor's brother Vsevolod and from the Vsevolod of unit 9 (see note)
glossary.мстиславичи: Мстиславичи — the Mstislavichi (nom. pl.); 'the three Mstislavichi,' cousins of Ingvar and Vsevolod, usually taken as sons of Mstislav Iziaslavich, from the same Volhynian branch as Roman (unit 20) — their exact identity is debated (see note)
glossary.худа: худъ — poor, mean (gen. sg. neut., agreeing with гнѣзда)
glossary.шестокрилци: шестокрилецъ — six-winged one (nom. pl.); most likely echoes the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6 as an exalted epithet, rather than a literal count of six princes (see note)
glossary.расхытисте: расхытити — you seized, snatched away (aorist 2pl; here for a group of five, carrying the plural aorist ending, not a dual — see note)
glossary.ляцкіи: ляцкый — Lyakh, Polish (nom. pl., adj.); from Ляхъ, the old term for a Pole (see note)
glossary.святъславлича: Святъславличь — Svyatoslavich, son of Svyatoslav (gen. sg.); patronymic; spelled here with ъ after т, «Святъславлича» — the refrain's third and final sounding, closing part 6, unlike «Святславлича» without ъ in units 15 and 19 — a small, real spelling inconsistency of the 1800 print, kept as printed (see note)
